[Submitted on 14 Oct 2026]

# Title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation

Authors: Kaixiang Zhao , Tianrun Yu , Shangzhe Li , Yuxiao Yang , Amanda Hughes , Weitong Zhang , Taylor W. Killian
View a PDF of the paper titled Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation, by Kaixiang Zhao and 6 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.

# Title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Authors: Linhao Zhong , Bozhen Fang , Xuehao Wang , Duochao Shi , Zekai Luo , Guangming Yao , Yi Yuan , Hao Chen , Jingdong Chen , Chunhua Shen
View a PDF of the paper titled More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning, by Linhao Zhong and 9 other authors

View PDF

Abstract: Self-distillation in agentic reinforcement learning has produced a growing number of methods. However, existing evaluations often reuse published baseline scores under differing experimental conditions, provide few direct comparisons among contemporaneous methods, and give limited attention to training stability and computational cost. These limitations obscure the source of reported gains and the practical strengths and weaknesses of competing methods. Costly agent training further motivates a common basis for comparison. To address these gaps, we compare ten representative methods against GRPO on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes. Our study comprises 132 training runs totaling 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluations over eight rollout seeds for the pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods. Beyond final task performance, we examine training progress, stability, and measured computational cost. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, gains over GRPO remain limited in scope, with no method consistently outperforming it across settings. Second, strong final performance can mask unstable training. Third, additional training cost does not consistently translate into better performance. We establish this benchmark to support fair, comprehensive comparison and guide future research toward reliable and cost-effective improvements in agent training. Project page: this https URL

CoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out.

Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US Federal Trade Commission has sent civil subpoenas to AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, seeking documents about safety incidents, Axios reported on Wednesday, citing a person
Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US Federal Trade Commission has sent civil subpoenas to AI giants Anthropic and OpenAI, seeking documents about safety incidents, Axios reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter.
The probe comes amid mounting AI safety concerns after models reportedly hacked websites and behaved deceptively or aggressively in testing, highlighting the risks of increasingly autonomous systems and the adequacy of safeguards against harm.
Last month, Reuters reported that the FTC planned an industry-wide investigation into AI companies.
The FTC also plans to compel executives at top AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research group METR to testify.
Advertisement

The FTC, OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Axios report.
The regulator's demands run to more than 50 pages each and seek information on security incidents, safeguards, marketing materials and privacy policies, the news website reported.
The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to take reasonable measures to secure consumers' data.
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson suggested in an interview with Reuters last month that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any harm they cause.
(Reporting by Anusha Shah and Harshita Mary Varghese in Bengaluru; editing by Leroy Leo and Saumyadeb Chakrabarty)

Seven Senate Democrats, led by Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden, wrote to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking whether the company used federal research tax credits to offset the cost of its AI data centers. The letter is dated October 13, 2026, and was made public on October 14 (sources differ slightly on the release date).

- **The core question:** The senators are asking whether Meta told the IRS that its AI data centers were experimental "pilot models" to qualify for the credit. Their letter cites published reports indicating Meta characterized its AI data centers to the IRS that way. The reporting behind it comes from a New York Times report from September 30.
- **The dollar figures:** Meta's filings indicate the credit reduced its federal income tax liability by $6.6 billion from 2023 through 2025. Annual claims were roughly $700 million in 2023, $2 billion in 2024, and $3.9 billion in 2025, with some outlets rounding the last figure to nearly $4 billion.
- **Their argument:** The senators say the credit is meant for experimental work with high technical uncertainty, and that data center hardware relies on proven technology and would not normally qualify. They say the approach violates "the spirit and, potentially, the letter" of the tax law.
- **Scale:** The letter cites Joint Committee on Taxation estimates that the credit cost the government about $32 billion in 2025, which would make Meta's share more than 10% of claims.
- **Other questions:** The letter also asks about $4.1 billion in stock-based compensation to Zuckerberg that Meta claimed as qualified research expenses.
- **Deadline and status:** The senators want answers no later than October 31, 2026. These are questions, not findings. The company's specific eligibility claims remain disputed, and the senators' questions do not constitute a formal finding of tax-law violations.

Anthropic has told prospective investors that revenue in the third quarter surged 45% from the prior quarter, two people who attended an investor day said, a move that could assuage market concerns about the huge costs of developing AI systems.

Third-quarter revenue rose to $16.8 billion from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $4.7 billion in the first quarter, the people said.

Anthropic told the group the company was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter, they added.

The meeting in San Francisco was meant to familiarise prospective Anthropic investors with the company before its highly anticipated IPO.

The IPO is expected to precede a public listing by rival OpenAI, making Anthropic an early test of investor appetite for loss-making AI developers investing heavily to pursue massive scale. Its public-market debut is likely to be pushed until after the November US midterm elections, Reuters has reported.

Attendees at yesterday's event met with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and came away optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability, a few of them told Reuters as they left its headquarters in the evening.

Amodei reiterated the company’s focus on AI safety but avoided mentioning threats of human extinction, one person in the group said.

In its prospectus seen by Reuters last month, Anthropic warned that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

Anthropic executives yesterday, however, talked about how the company was using its AI to help its own business including designing a custom chip. The company handed out hats to the attendees, some of which read "thinking."

Anthropic could see its annual revenue run rate reach $110 billion by the end of the year, according to estimates from analysts who met with company executives earlier this week.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Scrutiny of AI companies' finances has intensified as they pour money into chips, data centres and computing power needed to develop and operate increasingly powerful models.

Targeting a valuation of over $2 trillion, Anthropic is seeking to convince investors that its breakneck revenue growth can eventually outrun the enormous costs of building and running AI systems.

Last year, Anthropic's revenue increased twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, Reuters reported exclusively last month.

The company has committed at least $518 billion over a decade for cloud services, computing and infrastructure.

Founded by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. Its expansion has been underpinned by Alphabet's Google and Amazon, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors.

Anthropic has also sought to distinguish itself through its focus on AI safety, warning of the dangers posed by increasingly capable systems even as it competes in the race to develop and commercialise more powerful models.

results:
TrendForce's latest forecast (late September 2026) projects **further memory contract price increases in Q4 2026, but at a slower pace than earlier in the year**, driven mainly by AI server demand.

- **DRAM:** Conventional DRAM prices are projected to rise 10–15% QoQ. Enterprise SSDs are the only category expected to see price growth accelerate due to strong demand from CSPs.
- **NAND:** Overall NAND Flash contract prices are projected to increase 15–20% QoQ.
- **Server demand:** CSPs and server OEMs are increasing bit procurement to meet growing RDIMM demand for general servers supporting agentic AI workloads.
- **Supply:** TrendForce projects bit demand to grow by more than 80% YoY in 2026, and most of the additional supply has already been committed.
- **Consumer pushback:** Notebook inventories are increasingly reflecting higher component costs in the fourth quarter, weighing on end-market sales.

For context, the Q3 2026 forecast was higher: conventional DRAM contract prices were forecast to rise 13–18% QoQ in 3Q26, while NAND Flash contract prices were expected to increase 10–15%. The Q4 forecast is also described as moderating partly because substantial increases were already priced in during previous quarters.

Caveats: these are forecasts, not realized October contract prices, and I found no October 2026 contract-price data itself. One Evertiq table reads "Up 18~13%" for Q3 NAND, which looks like a typo; TrendForce's own Q3 figure is 10–15%. Some of the Q4 coverage is secondary (Sammy Fans, Evertiq, DEV Community) and relies on TrendForce's release.

Defense tech startup Anduril will give employees a chance to sell stock through a tender offer that would value the company at roughly $90 billion, CNBC has confirmed.
Bloomberg was the first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter. Anduril confirmed the report to CNBC.

Employees participating in the offering can sell shares at $94.80 apiece. The offer, which opened on Oct. 13 and closes Nov. 9, is capped at $1.3 billion, according to the report.
Bloomberg reported that employees in 16 countries are eligible to participate.
Anduril has been a major winner of the growing U.S. defense tech boom and President Donald Trump 's plans to reindustrialize the U.S. military. In May, the company closed a $5 billion funding round that doubled its valuation to $61 billion.
Co-founder and Oculus headset creator Palmer Luckey is among a growing group of defense tech leaders taking on advisory roles in Washington as they compete for key Department of Defense contracts.
This month, the company inked a U.S. Navy shipyard contract worth up to $2.9 billion, shortly after Luckey was named a co-director of Project Meridian, which aims to develop and scale military capabilities. SpaceX rocket maker CEO Elon Musk also joined the initiative.
Founded in 2017, Anduril has gained prominence for its drones, augmented reality headsets and AI software it's developing for the U.S. government and allied governments. Last month, the company made headlines after Iran said it had captured one of its underwater vehicles.

results:
I found no October 2026 figures. The most recent official numbers are from the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, which was released in April 2026.

- **FBI figures:** The report tracked AI-related fraud as its own category for the first time. It recorded 22,364 complaints and over $893 million in losses tied to AI-assisted scams in a single year. Malwarebytes gives the exact figure as $893,346,472 in AI-related scam losses.
- **Family-emergency scams:** The FBI's "distress scam" category covers voice cloning that impersonates a relative in crisis. These accounted for more than $5 million in confirmed losses.
- **Older adults:** According to the same study, older adults are the most frequently targeted group. One consumer-advice site says adults over 60 accounted for over $352 million of it.
- **FTC:** I found no FTC total for voice cloning losses. One source says the FTC has been sounding the alarm on this specific scam for years.

The FBI's $893 million is only reported losses, and these figures represent only the reported losses, which may well be the proverbial tip of the iceberg.

Be cautious with the much larger global figures circulating online, such as a claimed $4.20 billion annual loss. They come from a vendor-style blog that cites several organizations without clear sourcing, so I would not rely on them without checking the original research.

**Detection rate:** The post says the behavior appears "in only about 1 to 2 in 1,000 rollouts." Sequence models reveal diagnosis accumulation pathways beyond comorbidity burden in population-scale hospital data

Download PDF

# Abstract
Aging trajectories vary among individuals of similar age and disease burden. Comorbidity indices, e.g. the Elixhauser index, aggregate recorded conditions into a single score, but discard the timing, sequence, and pace of morbidity accumulation. Here we ask whether longitudinal hospital diagnosis histories contain information beyond age, sex, and comorbidity burden, and where it is concentrated. Using 13 years of Austrian inpatient data covering 7.4 million patients, we trained a visit-level contrastive transformer to encode diagnosis sequences and inter-admission timing into patient-history embeddings. In a downstream cohort of 1.7 million individuals, the embedding model improved prediction of in-hospital death over the Elixhauser-based comorbidity model, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.879 versus 0.866 (AUC gain = 0.0132, 95% CI 0.0118–0.0144). Across 130 incident ICD-10 disease-block outcomes, the embedding model had higher AUC for 93 outcomes, with a modest median gain of 0.006. Gains were concentrated in mental, musculoskeletal, nervous system, and metabolic disorders. We then evaluated event-free survival, defined as remaining alive without accumulating a second unrecorded ICD-10 disease block. The embedding model achieved an AUC of 0.726 versus 0.722 for the comorbidity model. However, among patients with similar age, sex, and comorbidity-model risk, those assigned high residual risk had 127–181 fewer event-free days over five years and observed event rates comparable to low-residual-risk patients more than a decade older. Together, these findings link the embedding’s signal to the breadth, recency, and pace of prior disease accumulation.

# Abstract
Although AI tools for neuroimaging show considerable promise in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of neurodegenerative disorders, their uptake in memory clinics has been limited. A key barrier is lack of consensus on their effective design and implementation. Here we establish expert consensus on the specific goals, usage and challenges of AI tools for neuroimaging in the memory clinic using a Delphi process. Sixteen experts from clinical, academic, and industry backgrounds participated in three rounds of questionnaires, coordinated by the Imaging Working Group of the Deep Dementia Phenotyping (DEMON) network, with support from a patient and public involvement representative. Consensus was reached on eight statements covering four themes: purpose, quality, interactions with clinicians and memory clinics, and privacy and ethics. Implementation of these recommendations will further the adoption of AI neuroimaging tools from research to clinical practice, improving diagnostic and care pathways for patient benefit.

# Abstract
Medical AI requires governance preserving safety during continuous improvement. FDA Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCP) and EU post-market surveillance address iterative updates but lack operational tooling. We present AEGIS, an internal governance and post-market-monitoring infrastructure designed to support the documentation of predetermined governance pathways for PCCP and Medical Devices Regulation alignment. AEGIS comprises dataset assimilation and retraining, model monitoring, and conditional decision-making modules. It utilizes a four-category taxonomy (APPROVE, CONDITIONAL APPROVAL, CLINICAL REVIEW, REJECT) and an independent ALARM signal. Instantiating AEGIS for sepsis prediction (PhysioNet) and brain-tumor segmentation (BraTS) exercised all decision categories, successfully routing failures to the critical REJECT + ALARM state (no deployable model; released model at risk). On real cross-site data, drift detection ROC-AUC rose from 0.82 to 1.00, reliably triggering near 500-patient batches with zero false alarms. This proof-of-concept utilizes illustrative clinical models; drift scoring quantifies covariate shift only, leaving concept drift for future work.

**Publication date:** October 14, 2026 (by Madlin Mekelburg and Georgia Fearn, Bloomberg, republished by Claims Journal)

**Case:** *Apple v. Liu*, No. 5:26-cv-07078, U.S. District Court, Northern District of California (San Jose Division). Judge Edward Davila is presiding.

**Background**
- Apple sued OpenAI, its hardware chief, and a former iPhone hardware engineer, Chang Liu, in July. Apple alleges they conspired to extract confidential information from former Apple employees about product design, manufacturing, components, testing, and supply chain.
- The dispute comes despite a two-year partnership that built ChatGPT into Apple software, and as hundreds of Apple employees have left for OpenAI.
- OpenAI denies the allegations and says Apple is trying to discourage employees from leaving for a competitor.
- Bloomberg reported that OpenAI's first consumer device will be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker priced above $300.

**What the hearing covers**
1. **Apple's preliminary injunction request:** Apple wants an order barring OpenAI from using confidential information it obtained from Apple and from seeking further private details. Apple says OpenAI used job interviews, where candidates allegedly were asked to bring prototypes and "design artifacts," to elicit proprietary information. If granted, the order would remain in place while the lawsuit proceeds.
2. **OpenAI's motion to dismiss:** OpenAI argues Apple has not identified specific stolen trade secrets, only broad categories of hardware development information.

On Tuesday, Davila also ordered OpenAI to speed up the production of documents related to the alleged theft.

**Statements from both sides**
- **Apple:** In its suit, Apple said OpenAI is exploiting the information to "advance OpenAI's efforts to enter the consumer hardware market." Apple also says Liu's personal iCloud material is "entirely separate" from its core claim that he later used an authentication flaw to access Apple's network storage.
- **OpenAI:** In an October filing, the company said it is "developing a new family of devices designed for the AI era" and has "no need or desire for Apple's trade secrets." OpenAI also argues the lawsuit reveals weaknesses in Apple's security and HR practices, including an authentication error that let Liu keep access after he left.

results:
I found no bill introduced on October 14, 2026. The closest match is the Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act, introduced around October 1, 2026, and the other results are from earlier in 2026.

- **Protecting Kids from Human-Like Chatbots Act (House, ~Oct. 1, 2026):** Reps. Doris Matsui, George Whitesides, Mike Kennedy, and Mariannette Miller-Meeks introduced it. It would bar chatbots from using human-like behavior toward minors by default, and it targets chatbot design rather than access or age verification. This legislation protects kids by prohibiting chatbots from communicating by default in a human-like way with minors.
- **GUARD Act (Senate, introduced October 2025):** Sen. Josh Hawley's bill would bar AI companion chatbots for users under 18 and requires age verification. It was advancing to the U.S. Senate after the chamber's Judiciary Committee voted unanimously in favor of it in May 2026.
- **SAFE KIDS Act (Senate, June 23, 2026):** Sens. John Curtis and Adam Schiff introduced it. It would require chatbot providers to create safeguards before making technology available to children, bar advertising to children and prevent chatbots from creating sexual deepfakes and copying human emotions.
- **CHATBOT Act (Senate):** Sen. Ted Cruz and Sens. Brian Schatz, Curtis, and Schiff introduced it. It would require AI companies to establish "family accounts" for parents to manage access and usage of AI chatbots by their children. I didn't find its introduction date.
- **CHAT Act 2.0 (Senate):** Sens. Andy Kim and Jon Husted introduced it. It would create a three-tier framework that applies appropriate safeguards based on a chatbot's intended purpose, covering educational, companion, and health chatbots. I didn't find its introduction date.

If you need the October 14 bill specifically, check congress.gov for bills introduced that day, since this search didn't surface one.

HEADLINE: Noma Labs discloses "SneakPeek" exploit chain in Claude Code Desktop preview pane, CVSS 8.7
PUBLISHED: October 14, 2026, 09:00 ET (PR Newswire)
SOURCES:
Noma Security (PR Newswire) | https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/noma-labs-uncovers-critical-security-vulnerabilities-in-claude-code-desktop-app-cvss-8-7-302908539.html | primary

Dark Reading | https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/new-anthropic-sneakpeek-silent-zero-click-threat | report
FACTS:
- Noma says the exploit chain, named "SneakPeek," was rated CVSS 8.7 (High) and let an attacker run arbitrary JavaScript and steal local data including API keys, cloud credentials, SSH keys and OAuth session tokens by getting the app's preview pane to render a poisoned file (Noma release).
- Noma names three combining gaps: files over 256KB loaded without the Content Security Policy applied to smaller files; `file://` loading gave the renderer direct local filesystem access; and the request filter meant to block `file://` access was inactive during static file rendering (Noma release).
- CSO Online reports files under 256KB were loaded as base64 `data:` URLs with a strict CSP that blocked scripts, while larger files were loaded as `file://` URLs, bypassing that protection; CVSS 8.7 (v4.0) was assigned by Anthropic, and no CVE ID was available at publication.
- Noma's disclosure timeline: report and PoC submitted July 4, 2026; Anthropic triaged, assigned CVSS 8.7 and deployed an initial mitigation July 9, 2026; on July 24, 2026 Noma demonstrated a bypass using file reads inside a Web Worker spawned from a `blob:` URL; Anthropic confirmed the bypass August 5, 2026; final patch verified and deployed August 17, 2026 (Noma release).
- CSO Online says Anthropic did not respond to its request for comment; Noma's Eli Ainhorn said Anthropic "confirmed they are preparing a GitHub Security Advisory and have requested a CVE for it."

# How consumer tech company Whoop is building for Medicare patients

# Under Medicare’s ACCESS pilot, Whoop will provide patients with a wearable, a 12-month subscription, and clinician support

Ami Bhatt, Whoop’s chief medical officer, speaks with STAT’s Mario Aguilar at the STAT Summit in Boston on Wednesday. Maura Wayman for STAT

By Katie Palmer
Oct. 14, 2026

Health Tech Correspondent

Katie Palmer

-
[email protected]

Katie covers the impact of health technology on patients, clinicians, and businesses. Her stories explore the price tag of clinical AI, digital health at the FDA, and the boom in direct-to-consumer telehealth. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at palmer.01.

Whoop has never been known for marketing to an older population. Performance athletes headline ads for the wearable company, which aims to turn continuous streams of physiological data into useful insights for behavior change — mostly, for a young, fit customer base.

But this year, Whoop became one of the first consumer wearable companies to be accepted into Medicare’s ACCESS program , making it available at no cost to many traditional Medicare patients ages 65 and up. On Wednesday, at the STAT Summit in Boston, Whoop’s newly appointed chief medical officer Ami Bhatt spoke about how the company is moving to build experiences — and demonstrate outcomes — for a very different population.
Advertisement

“Number one on our roadmap — and I think I’m allowed to say this, if I’m not, I’m saying it — is simplification of the app,” said Bhatt, who previously chaired the Food and Drug Administration’s digital health advisory committee and served as the American College of Cardiology’s chief innovation officer. Surveys suggest, said Bhatt, that even members of the Silent Generation, who are older than 80 today, trust their clinicians with their data. “It’s not that they’re averse to giving data,” she said. “It’s how easy can we make it for that population to be able to share their data.”

Bhatt said that Whoop, which recently raised $575 million from investors including Mayo Clinic and the sovereign wealth fund of Qatar, is working with the National Council on Aging and AARP to think about how to personalize the product to older adults’ individual priorities. “For each of us, how we feel, how we perform, how we age, we have our own goals,” said Bhatt. “The thing is, we don’t want to decide for you what that is.”

The goals are less diffuse for the 10-year pilot ACCESS program, which published a directory of initial participants last month. Through those 55 companies, Medicare patients can access chronic condition management for little or no cost — Whoop serves patients with high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity, and prediabetes — and Medicare will pay the companies based on their health outcomes. Whoop will provide patients with a wearable, a 12-month subscription to its app, and access to clinicians who can help them make sense of their data and offer advice.
Advertisement

“The goal is, how do we bring technology closer to the patient, but not put the cost on the patient — rather, put the demand on the company,” said Bhatt. “Whoop takes responsibility for, in 12 months, I am going to make these people better. I’m going to show you outcomes in the Medicare population who have these risk factors to demonstrate that my technology can help them engage in their own health.” To receive full payment under the ACCESS model, Whoop will be required to show that it improved or controlled measures tied to its patients’ chronic conditions, including blood pressure, hemoglobin A1C, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.

Bhatt said it was her role to help the company — which until recently focused on selling a product intentionally binned in the wellness category — develop and demonstrate those kinds of outcomes that bring them closer to clinical practice. The company just this year announced the ability for users to discuss their wearable data with clinicians , shortly before the FDA closed its warning letter that had initially said Whoop’s blood pressure-estimating feature qualified as a medical device — not a wellness feature.

While Whoop demonstrates good patient engagement, said Bhatt — users check the app eight times a day, on average — research into the original “wearable” for diabetes, continuous glucose monitors, suggests that engagement doesn’t necessarily translate to better health outcomes.

“In order to actually create personalized health at a population level, you need to start thinking about outcomes,” said Bhatt. “Can we show that we decrease blood pressure by five millimeters of mercury in individuals on Whoop — which, by the way, we have shown — so that we can say, hey, the outcome of cardiovascular disease and stroke, we know that outcome is better.”

Making AI work in healthcare

Download PDF

Download PDF

Drawing on experiences across diverse settings, this issue of Nature Medicine explores the challenges of and lessons learned from the deployment of artificial intelligence models into healthcare.

Advances in machine learning and generative artificial intelligence (AI) have produced tools that can potentially support an ever-expanding range of clinical tasks, from the interpretation of medical images to assisting clinicians in documenting and making decisions about patient care. Thus, AI technologies are being deployed into healthcare at a pace rarely seen for new medical innovations. In the USA, the Food and Drug Administration has begun a pilot program 1 for deploying AI clinical decision support tools before they are authorized, while over 800 healthcare institutions 2 , 3 have already deployed China’s DeepSeek model after its release. Yet a gap remains between AI hype and clinical reality.

Evidence remains limited on whether the deployment of these tools is having any real impact on patients, healthcare providers or health systems. A survey has already found that over 90% of US health systems have begun deploying AI tools for tasks such as radiology and clinical documentation, and 53% or less found these tools to be highly useful 4 .

Many of these implementation challenges stem from a disconnect between how AI is evaluated in research and how it is ultimately used in clinical practice. AI models often achieve impressive performance metrics in retrospective evaluation and reader studies, but these results do not necessarily translate into clinical value unless they are integrated into clinical workflows. Drawing on their experience developing an AI eye-care system in China, Yan et al. found that the AI technology was feasible only when embedded at every stage of the care pathway, emphasizing that successful AI deployment depends on more than model performance alone.

A related challenge is that different healthcare systems vary considerably in their resources, readiness of data infrastructure, models of care and workforce capacity. As a result, technologies that are feasible in one hospital setting may need to be substantially adapted to be implemented effectively elsewhere. Kabukye et al. highlight this challenge in low- and middle-income countries, where limited computational resources and shortages of specialists mean that AI systems will need to be redesigned as ‘frugal’ solutions tailored to local needs. Adaptation of medical AI to different healthcare contexts is especially important when considering international scale up. For example, Tiwari et al. report that deploying the same diabetic retinopathy AI system across India, Thailand and Australia required vastly different implementation strategies shaped by local healthcare priorities and clinical workflows.

HEADLINE: Transformer trained on 7.4 million Austrian inpatients beats comorbidity index at predicting in-hospital death
PUBLISHED: 14 Oct 2026 (npj Digital Medicine)

- Using 13 years of Austrian inpatient data covering 7.4 million patients, the authors trained a visit-level contrastive transformer to encode diagnosis sequences and inter-admission timing into patient-history embeddings (abstract).

Sequence models reveal diagnosis accumulation pathways beyond comorbidity burden in population-scale hospital data

Download PDF

# Abstract
Aging trajectories vary among individuals of similar age and disease burden. Comorbidity indices, e.g. the Elixhauser index, aggregate recorded conditions into a single score, but discard the timing, sequence, and pace of morbidity accumulation. Here we ask whether longitudinal hospital diagnosis histories contain information beyond age, sex, and comorbidity burden, and where it is concentrated. Using 13 years of Austrian inpatient data covering 7.4 million patients, we trained a visit-level contrastive transformer to encode diagnosis sequences and inter-admission timing into patient-history embeddings. In a downstream cohort of 1.7 million individuals, the embedding model improved prediction of in-hospital death over the Elixhauser-based comorbidity model, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.879 versus 0.866 (AUC gain = 0.0132, 95% CI 0.0118–0.0144). Across 130 incident ICD-10 disease-block outcomes, the embedding model had higher AUC for 93 outcomes, with a modest median gain of 0.006. Gains were concentrated in mental, musculoskeletal, nervous system, and metabolic disorders. We then evaluated event-free survival, defined as remaining alive without accumulating a second unrecorded ICD-10 disease block. The embedding model achieved an AUC of 0.726 versus 0.722 for the comorbidity model. However, among patients with similar age, sex, and comorbidity-model risk, those assigned high residual risk had 127–181 fewer event-free days over five years and observed event rates comparable to low-residual-risk patients more than a decade older. Together, these findings link the embedding’s signal to the breadth, recency, and pace of prior disease accumulation.
